supported_facts: AP reported in April 2017 that U.S. imports of Ivanka Trump merchandise had risen an estimated 166% over the prior year, based on shipping data; the brand said its revenues were up 21%.
The reporting described record sales and provisional Chinese trademark approvals as separate facts.
unsupported_original_claims: The 166% statistic is an import estimate, not a reported increase in brand sales or profits during the first year of the presidency.
The sources do not establish that the White House role caused the import change or that it was an emoluments violation.
access_notes: Read AP reporting syndicated by CBS News and AP; both returned text. The sources distinguish imports from revenue.
corrected_title: Ivanka Trump Merchandise Imports Rose an Estimated 166% as Brand Revenue Increased 21%
corrected_claim: Associated Press reporting in April 2017 said U.S. imports of Ivanka Trump merchandise, almost all from China, rose an estimated 166% over the prior year. The company reported a 21% revenue increase, while sales reached record levels. The 166% figure measures imports, not brand sales or profits. The same reporting described provisional Chinese trademark approvals separately; it does not show that Ivanka Trump's White House role caused the commercial growth.
exact_gap: No reviewed source supports the stored 166% sales/profit figure or proves a causal link between her advisory role and the brand's revenue or imports.

supported_facts: The 2018 superseding indictment alleged that Manafort generated tens of millions of dollars from Ukraine work, routed more than $75 million through offshore accounts, and—with Rick Gates's assistance—laundered more than $30 million in income concealed from U.S. authorities.
unsupported_original_claims: The reviewed indictment does not support the headline's exact $65 million total as payments specifically from Rinat Akhmetov and Viktor Yanukovych.
The indictment is an allegation; it does not establish every allegation in this synopsis as an adjudicated fact.
access_notes: The originally supplied DOJ file URL returned an Akamai access page. A separate official DOJ superseding-indictment PDF was readable and provides the narrower allegations cited here.
corrected_title: Manafort Indictment Alleges More Than $30 Million in Concealed Ukraine-Related Income
corrected_claim: A 2018 superseding indictment alleged that Paul Manafort generated tens of millions of dollars from political consulting and lobbying in Ukraine, routed more than $75 million through offshore accounts, and concealed more than $30 million in income with Rick Gates's assistance. These are allegations in the charging document. It does not establish the original headline's $65 million as payments specifically from Rinat Akhmetov and Viktor Yanukovych.
exact_gap: No reviewed source supports the precise $65 million payer attribution. The indictment supports the narrower alleged offshore-income figures, not a conclusive finding about every claim in the frozen synopsis.

supported_facts: At the July 12, 2022 committee hearing, Vice Chair Liz Cheney said Trump had attempted to call a witness who had not yet appeared publicly; the witness did not answer and notified a lawyer.
Cheney said the committee supplied the contact information to the Justice Department; Reuters reported the same account.
unsupported_original_claims: The reviewed sources do not support the full year-long composite claim about attacks on all Republican witnesses, systematic pressure not to cooperate, or threats resulting from Trump's statements.
A committee referral is not a finding that Trump committed obstruction.
access_notes: Read Reuters' contemporaneous report and the House hearing transcript; the transcript records Cheney's statement as an attributed allegation.
corrected_title: January 6 Committee Refers Trump's Attempted Contact With a Witness to DOJ
corrected_claim: At a July 12, 2022 January 6 Committee hearing, Vice Chair Liz Cheney said Donald Trump had attempted to call a witness who had not yet testified publicly. She said the witness did not answer, informed a lawyer, and that the committee referred the information to the Justice Department. Reuters reported the statement. It documents the reported contact and referral, not an adjudicated finding of witness intimidation or obstruction.
exact_gap: The evidence supports a discrete reported attempted call and DOJ referral. It does not establish the original claims of systematic intimidation, resulting threats, or the committee's referral as proof of criminal conduct.

supported_facts: The Washington Post reported that DOGE personnel sought access to IRS systems and taxpayer data as part of a government-wide review.
A February 20 report said Treasury and White House officials agreed to prohibit DOGE from accessing personal taxpayer data; the DOGE representative's access would be limited to anonymized data.
unsupported_original_claims: The sources do not establish that DOGE operatives accessed or reviewed individual tax returns of political opponents, Democratic donors or journalists.
The record's March date is wrong for the reported access request and limitation agreement.
access_notes: Read the two Washington Post reports through returned excerpts. The reports describe a request and a later restriction, not confirmed inspection of individual returns.
corrected_title: DOGE Sought IRS Data Access; Officials Agreed to Bar Access to Personal Tax Records
corrected_claim: In February 2025, DOGE personnel sought access to IRS systems during the administration's government-wide review. The Washington Post reported on February 20 that Treasury and White House officials agreed to bar DOGE from personal taxpayer data and limit its IRS representative to anonymized data. The reports document the access request and its restrictions, not access to or review of political opponents' individual returns.
exact_gap: No reviewed source documents DOGE viewing individual returns belonging to political opponents, donors or journalists. The evidence supports a request and negotiated access limits, rather than the alleged data breach.

supported_facts: Reuters reported that Trump launched large-scale U.S. strikes against the Houthis on March 15, 2025.
Reuters reported that a Houthi-run health ministry spokesperson gave an updated toll of at least 31 killed and 101 injured, mostly women and children; the toll was attributed to that authority.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited report does not support more than 80 deaths in the March 15 opening strikes; the 31-death toll is attributed to Houthi-run authorities, not independently verified by Reuters.
The source does not establish a specific civilian/fighter breakdown, absence of congressional authorization, strategic efficacy, or later campaign-wide casualty totals.
access_notes: Read Reuters' March 15 report, updated with a March 16 casualty figure; the reported toll is explicitly attributed to Houthi-run health authorities.
corrected_title: Trump Launches U.S. Strikes Against Houthis; Houthi Authorities Report 31 Killed
corrected_claim: The United States began large-scale strikes against Yemen's Houthis on March 15, 2025. Reuters reported that Houthi-run health authorities later gave a toll of at least 31 people killed and 101 injured, mostly women and children. The casualty count is attributed to those authorities and is not an independently verified March 15 total. This evidence does not support the frozen entry's figure of more than 80 deaths for that opening event.
exact_gap: The original combines a campaign-wide toll with the March 15 opening date. The reviewed source supports an attributed report of 31 deaths, but not the original 80-plus figure or casualty classification.

supported_facts: Reuters reported before the June 2024 presidential debate that Biden prepared at Camp David while Trump eschewed traditional mock-debate preparation and instead held informal policy discussions with advisers and allies.
unsupported_original_claims: The reviewed report does not verify Trump's 'natural instinct' quotation, repeated refusals across multiple debates, or dismissal of specific advisers.
It does not establish that preparation style caused factual errors or off-topic debate performance.
access_notes: Read Reuters' June 21, 2024 report; it supports a description of that debate-preparation period only.
corrected_title: Trump Uses Informal Policy Discussions Instead of Mock-Debate Preparation in June 2024
corrected_claim: Ahead of the June 2024 presidential debate, Donald Trump did not use traditional mock-debate sessions and instead held informal policy discussions with advisers and allies between campaign appearances, Reuters reported. The source documents this preparation approach for that debate; it does not verify the stored 'natural instinct' quote or show that the approach caused later debate errors.
exact_gap: The exact 'natural instinct' quote and the broader claims about repeated refusals, adviser disputes and debate consequences lack support in the reviewed source.

supported_facts: On December 17, 2016, President-elect Trump tweeted that China's seizure of a U.S. Navy underwater drone was 'unpresidented,' misspelling 'unprecedented.'
Contemporaneous reporting identifies the typo and public reaction; the tweet was later deleted and replaced with corrected wording.
unsupported_original_claims: The event date was December 17, not December 30, 2016.
The interpretation that the typo itself demonstrated a broader literacy or foreign-policy failure is commentary rather than an event fact.
access_notes: Read The World from PRX and The Guardian's contemporaneous reports; both returned text about the December 17 post.
corrected_title: Trump Tweets 'Unpresidented' in Post About China's Seizure of U.S. Navy Drone
corrected_claim: On December 17, 2016, President-elect Donald Trump criticized China's seizure of a U.S. Navy underwater drone in a tweet that misspelled 'unprecedented' as 'unpresidented.' Contemporaneous reporting documented the typo and the response it drew; reports also say the post was deleted and corrected. The event was on December 17, not the December 30 date in the frozen record.
exact_gap: The corrected event is supported, but the record's date is wrong and the typo alone does not establish broader claims about literacy, proofreading practices or the risks of social-media diplomacy.

supported_facts: The executive grant records a commutation of Kwame Kilpatrick's remaining sentence dated January 13, 2021; the White House announced it among the January 20 clemency actions.
Kilpatrick's convictions were not erased by the commutation. The January 20 White House statement gave a public explanation for the clemency.
unsupported_original_claims: Trump commuted Kilpatrick's sentence; he did not pardon him.
The statement that the White House gave no explanation is inaccurate.
The assertion that the action bypassed DOJ clemency review is not established by the reviewed clemency records.
access_notes: Read the White House release, DOJ commutations listing and signed executive grant; AP also reported Kilpatrick's release after the commutation.
The grant is dated January 13 while the administration's release is dated January 20; preserve that distinction.
corrected_title: Trump Commutes Kwame Kilpatrick's Sentence; White House Announces It on January 20
corrected_claim: President Trump signed an order commuting former Detroit mayor Kwame Kilpatrick's remaining prison sentence on January 13, 2021; the White House announced the action on January 20. The commutation ended his imprisonment but did not erase his convictions. The White House statement supplied its rationale, while the reviewed records do not establish whether the case followed a traditional DOJ clemency review.
exact_gap: The frozen entry conflates a commutation with a pardon and treats the announcement date as the grant date. The reviewed records do not substantiate the claim that the action bypassed DOJ review.

supported_facts: Reporting on April 1, 2025 described layoffs and leadership leave or reassignments across HHS, including NIH; approximately 1,200 NIH layoffs were planned, according to The Washington Post.
The Washington Post reported that NIAID director Jeanne Marrazzo was among the senior leaders affected.
unsupported_original_claims: The stored March date and claim that RFK Jr. personally fired dozens of top NIH scientists as one discrete action are not supported by the cited April 1 reporting.
The sources do not demonstrate that the changes crippled outbreak response or set biomedical research back a generation.
access_notes: The Washington Post item returned relevant excerpted text; AP's report confirms layoffs began at health agencies on April 1. The scale and projected numbers are attributed to reporting, not an official final tally.
corrected_title: April 2025 HHS Restructuring Includes NIH Layoffs and Senior-Leader Reassignments
corrected_claim: On April 1, 2025, layoffs and leadership reassignments began across HHS agencies during the administration's restructuring. The Washington Post reported that about 1,200 NIH layoffs were planned and that senior leaders were placed on leave or reassigned, including NIAID director Jeanne Marrazzo. These reports document a workforce action; they do not establish that it eliminated NIH's ability to respond to outbreaks or quantify long-term research effects.
exact_gap: The source supports April 1 layoffs and leadership changes, not the frozen March date, a personal firing of dozens of scientists by RFK Jr., or the claimed downstream effects on research and preparedness.

supported_facts: Reuters' July 11, 2025 profile describes White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller as a central figure driving and championing Trump's aggressive immigration agenda.
unsupported_original_claims: The reviewed source does not establish that Miller personally drafted every executive order, legal theory, administrative procedure and enforcement mechanism in the program.
The source does not substantiate the synopsis's specific claims about widespread due-process violations.
access_notes: Read the Reuters profile; its text supports Miller's central policy influence without assigning sole authorship of the full legal framework.
corrected_title: Reuters Describes Stephen Miller as a Central Driver of Trump's Immigration Agenda
corrected_claim: A July 2025 Reuters profile described White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller as a central figure driving and championing the Trump administration's aggressive immigration agenda. The report supports a claim about his influence and role, but not that he personally drafted every executive order, legal theory or operational procedure associated with the campaign.
exact_gap: A precise source for the original's comprehensive sole-author attribution and the cited due-process findings was not found in the reviewed evidence.
